title: The bridge
hookLine: a bridge over the fire, crossed by light

cards: Show us the straight path. Muslims say that line, from al-Fatiha, in their daily prayers; in Pickthall's translation it is simply "Show us the straight path." The Arabic for path there is sirat.

In the hadith about the Day of Resurrection, sirat names a path no one walks lightly: a bridge, laid over the fire, that people must cross. One word, then, for a path asked for in prayer and for a crossing made once.

teach.b: A long hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, describes it. A bridge is set over Hell, slippery, with hooks along it. People cross at very different speeds.
Some go over like the blink of an eye.
Some like lightning, some like the wind, some like fast horses or riding camels. Some come through safe, some come through scratched, and some fall.
In Sahih Muslim, Abu Sa'id adds something he says had reached him: that the bridge is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword. He's careful to say it reached him.

Another hadith in Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, says that on that day only the messengers will speak, and what they say is, in paraphrase: O Allah, keep safe, keep safe. Even the prophets, praying for the crossing.
So how does anyone get across?

teach.h: LIGHT BEFORE THEM, AND ON THEIR RIGHT.
teach.b: In Surah al-Hadid, Pickthall: on the day when the believers are seen, men and women, "their light shining forth before them and on their right hands." They cross by light.
The next verse has the hypocrites calling out to borrow some of that light, and being turned back. Light can't be borrowed on the Day. It has to be brought.
Where does it come from? A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives one answer: prayer is light, charity is proof, patience is brightness. So some teachers join the two sirats.
The straight path asked for in every prayer is practice for the bridge: walk it here by the light of what you do, and that light walks with you there.

how: Muslims ask for the straight path in al-Fatiha when they pray, and teach from the hadith that on the Day of Resurrection people will cross a bridge, the sirat, over the fire, by the light of their deeds.

o: the path, and the bridge over the fire that all must cross
the scale on which every deed is weighed on the Day
the light that believers carry in their right hands

p: light before them and on their right

s: in the hadith, everyone crosses the bridge at the same speed
some like the blink of an eye, some like lightning, wind, or horses; some are scratched, some fall.
sirat is the same word as the straight path of al-Fatiha
the path asked for in prayer, and the bridge on the Day.
in al-Hadid, the hypocrites can borrow the believers' light
they ask to borrow it and are turned back.

games.q: you're on the plain, in the dark, and someone ahead has light. you ask to borrow some. by al-Hadid, what happens?
o: they share it, and you cross together.
you're turned back: light can't be borrowed.
games.why: in al-Hadid the hypocrites ask to borrow light and are turned back. the light has to be brought, not borrowed.

practice: The hadith named three sources of light: prayer, charity, patience. Choose one, perhaps one prayer said slowly and on time if you pray, or a small gift given without fuss, or patience with one person who usually wears you down.
Then, with each out-breath, picture a little light gathering in front of you, enough to see a few steps ahead.

wordCard.voice: Sirat. The path; in the hadith, the bridge over the fire that all must cross on the Day, and the same word as the straight path of al-Fatiha. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a path, a way; the word in al-Fatiha and the name of the bridge.

carryVoice: Your line: cross with light. It can't be borrowed on the Day; it has to be brought. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.q: their light shining forth before them and on their right hands
